features.label: Need a thing; relative complement
features.description: Beðurfan takes a genitive of the thing needed in the selected ordinary frame, e.g. hwǣtes. In ðā ðing ðe wē beðurfon, ðā ðing is accusative object of buy, while invariant ðe supplies the dependency required by beðurfan within the relative. Its unchanged spelling does not make the internal dependency accusative. BT95 directly quotes this very Genesis43.4/8 clause; it also attests other government, so accusative alternatives are not globally impossible.

features.label: Swear oaths and report their content

prior_records.description: A simple preterite can express action earlier than another past viewpoint.

Cook188 expressly permits the simple preterite for all three past tenses. Thus37.6 first sętte, and40.4/6–8 simple preterites, can represent the English perfect without inventing new auxiliary-plus-participle cells. Analytic habban perfect is a defensible alternative where the precise participle is actually taught or supplied. An om.hath control reinforces a target; its absence is not a command to calque every English perfect.

paradigms.diagnostic_rule: Prefix fore- plus Cook123 sęcg(e)an. Select -ean/-eað; present2/3sg foresægst/foresægð and preterite foresægde/-st/-on. Uncontracted æ before gd stays unmarked as Cook prints sægde; contracted sāde is a separate documented alternative, not a license to lengthen *sǣgde. BT Supplement240 explicitly distinguishes having mentioned someone earlier from future prediction. Here use the past-reference sense with accusative person/topic and dative hearer.

teaching_records.description: Beðurfan takes a genitive of the thing needed in the selected ordinary frame, e.g. hwǣtes. In ðā ðing ðe wē beðurfon, ðā ðing is accusative object of buy, while invariant ðe supplies the dependency required by beðurfan within the relative. Its unchanged spelling does not make the internal dependency accusative. BT95 directly quotes this very Genesis43.4/8 clause; it also attests other government, so accusative alternatives are not globally impossible.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Oncnāwan in the selected recognition sense takes an accusative recognized person. The nominative recognizer controls the verb; a change of recognizer from ic to wē changes person/number independently of the object. Present cnāw-/cnǣw- and past cnēow- stay distinct.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Undōn means undo/open the tied sacks in45.8 and takes the accusative container. Present dēð and preterite dyde are different stems; plural preterite undydon follows the plural opener, not the number of sacks.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Swęrian/swerian takes accusative āðas as the sworn utterance. A dative recipient mīnum fæder48.1 needs no English to; ætforan us44.2 names the people in whose presence it was sworn. The reported content is a ðæt clause: mōsten gives past reported permission, brōhte a promised bringing viewed prospectively from the former oath. The two case frames are not interchangeable.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: 44.5 retains the explicitly required genitive demonstrative ðæs after giernan, followed by the content-explaining ðæt clause. Lǣdden is first-plural past subjunctive under the former desire; the second ðæt is a conjunction, not a second case-inflected demonstrative. The earlier genitive thing/person request frame alone did not teach this full propositional use.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Gedōn has accusative person hine plus agreeing accusative masculine singular glædne. In45.2 gedō is third-singular present subjunctive expressing the wish; it is not an imperative addressed to the named Lord. Wið ēow supplies the graciousness target, as the original hint expressly requires.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Āgiefan selects the returned person as accusative and the recipient as dative. Ēow and ēowerne brōðor have different roles. Present subjunctive āgiefe is in the final purpose clause, not merely an unexplained alternative ending.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Berēafian takes accusative person and genitive possessions in its selected active frame. In the passive the deprived person becomes the nominative subject, while genitive mīnra bearna remains.45.6 has genitive plural assena and ðinga; selfe agrees with accusative ūs in the following enslavement clause. BT Supplement81 gives this genitive construction and separately documents instrumental/dative alternatives, which must not be mislabeled impossible.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Hlystan governs genitive speech/content in45.7, as the explicit156 hint directs. Thus ūrre sprǣce is genitive feminine singular, distinct from accusative ūre sprǣce. The people beseech the steward (ðē accusative); ðū is the subject of subordinate hlyste.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: The selected ðēowian sense is enslave, with an accusative person. BT1056 senseII cites precisely Gen43.18, ðæt hē ūs ðēowige. The more common serve sense with different government remains separate. Our ðēowie normalizes the documented -ige/-ie variation under Cook119 and does not change tense or mood.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Bēodan takes a dative addressee in46.7 and48.8, as164 expressly directs. It can accompany a direct command or introduce ðæt plus subjunctive commanded action.47.11 intentionally retains present bīetst (commandest); the lookalike bīetst of bēatan is not the lexical identity here.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Lęcgean takes accusative things laid, with forð marking their presentation in46.3. Its source reading imperative lęcgeað is separately supplied; learning indicative plural lęcgeað does not by itself assign the command use.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Foresęcgean here means mention previously, not foretell the future. The invariant ðe is the mentioned person (accusative function), and mē the dative hearer. The English of is explicitly omitted. BT Supplement240 distinguishes the past-reference sense and illustrates a person mentioned earlier.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Ofðyncean is third-singular impersonal with dative experiencer ēow and a cause/content ðæt clause. Present subjunctive ofðynce gives nor let it grieve you; no separately invented personal subject it is needed. The plural experiencer does not demand a plural verb. The four-cell paradigm explicitly limits productive morphology to this impersonal construction.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: 48.6 extends the previously taught accusative feared-entity frame to the directly attested genitive frame: reflexive dative ēow plus nānes ðinges. Cook156h/159a explicitly gives ne ondrǣd ðū ðē ǣniges ðinges.46.1 has only the reflexive dative, with no expressed feared entity. This ēow is not an accusative object merely because its spelling is syncretic.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: In46.9 accusative neuter gōd is the good being repaid; mid yfele is the evil given in return. The recipient frame previously used for paying is not by itself this good-for-evil substitution frame. Wolden is third-plural past subjunctive inside the reported why-question; forgieldan is its plain infinitive.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: 46.9 when you have caught them concerns a future condition for the command to ask. The selected ðonne ðū hīe fō uses second-singular present subjunctive, following196b. There is no required present-perfect auxiliary. Original English says you, and the singular steward continues as addressee of Ārīs, gā and āsca.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: 47.3 retains195: in sīe hē ofslægen mid ðǣm ðe ðū hit finde, finde is second-singular present subjunctive within the relative governed by the hypothetical/optative context. Mid takes a dative associate; ðe is invariant. This is not a rule that every relative clause uses subjunctive.
teaching_records.lesson_placement: Before the earliest task that requires this construction; whole supplied help remains visible at every use.

teaching_records.description: Cook188 permits the simple preterite for English simple, perfect and pluperfect past. In45.8 cēapodon and ǣr sealdon give the anterior actions;46.9 fōron ... sumne dǣl ðæs weges conveys had gone without an unassigned intransitive habban perfect. Each clause remains present in the model.

teaching_records.description: Complete contrary condition and anterior result: if this delay were not, we would already have come a second time. Nǣre is ne+wǣre, third-singular past subjunctive; wǣren is first-plural past subjunctive. Cumen is a past participle with intransitive wesan, not the identically spelled present-subjunctive plural. Ōðre sīðe is adverbial instrumental singular, expressly176; the sīð hint names the lemma and does not suppress its ending. The entire combined construction and contracted form are supplied; no general counterfactual-perfect mastery is inferred.

audited_inflection_rules.text: Every class is already taught. New count nouns receive eight complete literal cells; selected mass/abstract nouns receive all four singular cells with their plural explicitly outside the assigned sense. No isolated needed case substitutes for a stated system.
Headword spelling and class evidence are source-specific. Complete tables are declared rule-derived; OCR, headword familiarity and prior display do not certify individual forms or senses.

Read actual prior entries before promotion. Preserve source-analysis strings and historical metadata separately; clǣnum records are matched using their explicit original gender description, and Hāl differs only in capitalization. The current cell analysis does not overwrite prior chapter history.
Keep strong noun theow-servant, adjective theow and weak noun theowa as distinct identities; also keep ealdor-chief separate from life, and weorth-price separate from verbs or adjective senses.
The exact source reading retains ðēowa manna and ðēowum mannum. Its whole expression is supplied with a bounded analysis; these noun tables do not automatically grant the construction.

Cook-recognized -ung oblique -a, feminine plural -e, adjective contractions and other independently evidenced variants are not errors solely because a different variant was selected; they do not count as independently taught unless explicitly recorded.

lexical_frames.label: Need a thing; relative complement
lexical_frames.description: Beðurfan takes a genitive of the thing needed in the selected ordinary frame, e.g. hwǣtes. In ðā ðing ðe wē beðurfon, ðā ðing is accusative object of buy, while invariant ðe supplies the dependency required by beðurfan within the relative. Its unchanged spelling does not make the internal dependency accusative. BT95 directly quotes this very Genesis43.4/8 clause; it also attests other government, so accusative alternatives are not globally impossible.

lexical_frames.label: Swear oaths and report their content

The reported content is a ðæt clause: mōsten gives past reported permission, brōhte a promised bringing viewed prospectively from the former oath. The two case frames are not interchangeable.

prior_records.description: A simple preterite can express action earlier than another past viewpoint.

Cook188 expressly permits the simple preterite for all three past tenses. Thus37.6 first sętte, and40.4/6–8 simple preterites, can represent the English perfect without inventing new auxiliary-plus-participle cells. Analytic habban perfect is a defensible alternative where the precise participle is actually taught or supplied. An om.hath control reinforces a target; its absence is not a command to calque every English perfect.

source_lines.source_with_note_markers: Sōðlice, mid-ðȳ-ðe ðæs cyninges dohtor geseah ðæt Apol-
lonius on eallum gōdum cræftum swā wel wæs getogen,[10]
ðā gefēoll hiere mōd on his lufe. Ðā, æfter ðæs bēorscipes
geęndunge, cwæð ðæt mǣden tō ðǣm cyninge: “Lēofa[11]
fæder, ðū līefdest mē, lȳtle[1] ǣr,[1] ðæt[2] ic[2] mōste[2] giefan
Apollonio swā-hwæt-swā ic wolde of ðīnum goldhorde.”
Arcestrates se cyning cwæð tō hiere: “Gief him swā-
hwæt-swā ðū wille.[3]” Hēo ðā swīðe blīðe ūtēode,[4] and
cwæð: “Lārēow[5] Apolloni, ic giefe ðē, be mīnes fæder
lēafe, twā hund punda[6] goldes,[7] and fēower hund punda[6]
gewihte[8] seolfres,[7] and ðone mǣstan dǣl dēorwurðes[9]
rēafes, and twēntig ðēowa[10] manna.[10]” And hēo ðā ðus
cwæð tō ðǣm ðēowum mannum: “Berað ðās ðing mid
ēow, ðe ic behēt Apollonio mīnum lārēowe, and lęcgeað
innan būre[11] beforan mīnum frēondum.” Ðis wearð ðā
ðus gedōn, æfter ðǣre cwēne hǣse[12]; and ealle ðā męnn
hiere giefa hęredon ðe[13] hīe gesāwon. Ðā sōðlice geęnd-
ode se gebēorscipe, and ðā męnn ealle ārison,[14] and
grētton ðone cyning and ðā cwēne, and bǣdon hīe
gesunde bēon,[15] and hām gewęndon. Ēac swilce Apol-
lonius cwæð: “Ðū gōda cyning, and earmra[16] gemiltsiend,
and ðū cwēn, lāre[16] lufiend, bēon gē gesunde.[17]” Hē
beseah ēac tō ðǣm ðēowum mannum, ðe ðæt mǣden him
forgiefen hæfde,[18] and him cwæð tō: “Nimað ðās ðing mid
ēow, ðe mē sēo cwēn forgeaf, and gān[1] wē sēcean ūre
giesthūs, ðæt wē mægen ūs[2] geręstan.”

U03-ADJ-USE.evidence_note: Strong/weak conditions and agreement. Cook says weak sometimes after possessives; this is not a universal possessive→weak rule.

U03-STRONG.evidence_note: Complete strong pattern, short/long stems, æ/a alternation, disyllabic syncope and optional loss of -u, -e stems, h-loss and consonant simplification.

U03-WEAK.evidence_note: Complete weak pattern. Selected ordinary Gpl -ra; -a/-ena are explicitly admitted alternatives. Comparative Gpl contraction is explained, not a license to invent arbitrary assimilation.

U03-COMPARE.evidence_note: Regular, umlaut and irregular degrees; comparative weak, superlative usually weak. Selected representative series below, not blanket mastery of all examples.

U03-ADVERB.evidence_note: Adverb formation and degree; wīd→wīde, swīð→swīðe very, sōð→sōðlice truly. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives or adverbs.

U03-NUMERAL.evidence_note: Cardinal/ordinal spellings and complete one/two/three rules; ordinals weak except ōðer.

U03-POSSESSIVE.evidence_note: Six agreeing first/second-person possessives; third-person genitives indeclinable. sīn not selected.

U03-DEMONSTRATIVE.evidence_note: Full that/this paradigms. Cook prints short-e ðes, not ðēs; selected double-s variants. Instrumental is reference recognition only.

U03-WRIGHT-USE.evidence_note: Positive/superlative predicate strong; eall and ōðer always strong. Full paradigms confirm agreement; mixed-gender predicate exception remains outside present tasks.

U03-WRIGHT-SYNCOPE.evidence_note: Long-disyllable syncope with retention before consonantal endings; analogical micles/miclum explicitly printed; hāligu and hālgu variants; -erra/-erre may simplify.

U03-WRIGHT-E.evidence_note: Full wilde pattern used by ūre, with its separate fem.Nsg exception in §464.

U03-WRIGHT-GEARU.evidence_note: Complete gearu strong pattern (gearone, gearore, gearora; gearw- before vowel) and weak gearwa/gearwe.

U03-WRIGHT-HEAH.evidence_note: Complete contracted hēah strong pattern and weak hēa, hēan. Selected hēanne/hēarre/hēarra/hēaum; source also gives simpler variants.

U03-WRIGHT-COMPARE.evidence_note: Comparatives weak; irregular series and their variants. Does not individually attest every derived case.

U03-WRIGHT-NUMERAL.evidence_note: Plural ān rare with different distributive sense, not cardinal one with plural count nouns; 4–19 generally uninflected before a noun, with separately conditioned inflection outside this unit.

U03-WRIGHT-POSSESSIVE.evidence_note: uncer/incer/ēower explicitly like hālig; ūre like wilde except F.Nsg ūre. ūrre/ūrra may simplify. Combined with §§429/431 yields transparent pattern-derived cells.

U03-WRIGHT-ADVERB.evidence_note: Exact wel/bet/betst and regular -or/-ost pattern; Cook hook spelling selected for bęt/bętst.

U03-THAN.evidence_note: Attested Beowulf469 comparison Sē wæs betere þonne iċ! provides a nominative standard after than with unexpressed repeated copula. Bounded analogous composition, not a claim that all than-constructions take nominative.

U12-ROOT-BT-HABBAN-AGREEMENT.claim: The entry distinguishes uninflected participles from inflected and mixed usage with habban. The object may be described by an accusative participle; the finite auxiliary still agrees with its subject. Bare and agreeing realizations are evidenced alternatives, not an exceptionless mapping from English perfect grammar.

exact_examples.analysis: Plural finite subject Hie contrasts with singular accusative hine/ofslægenne. This is evidence for object-linked participial inflection, not participle agreement with the finite subject.

exact_examples.analysis: The coordinated example combines a bare participle with an inflected accusative-masculine participle referring to the object aldor.

U16-MT-P114.inspection_scope: Firstcolumn14.8: Iohannes heafod þæs fulluhteres. Firstcolumn14.10: beheafdode Iohannem on þam cwerterne. The genitive Iohannes and accusative Iohannem are directly attested; the rightcolumn variant Iohanne is not silently substituted.
U16-MT-P114.declared_normalization: Retain the attested endings, writing initial J in Johannes/Johannem solely to follow Cook’s printed Johannes hint. No vowel quantity is inferred and no complete Latin proper-name system is assigned.
U16-MT-P114.teaching_scope: Supply Johannes as the genitive in36.9 and Johannem as the accusative in36.10; identify both roles explicitly.

U16-C06-REWARD.editorial_treatment: Documented correction C06, with exact source prompt and primary evidence preserved separately.
U16-C06-REWARD.inspection_scope: The printed weak headword/class belong to a verb meaning sin or fail in duty. Repay/reward requires the distinct strong gyldan verb. The source English, original hint and original image are all retained; only modern guidance is corrected.

supporting_primary_evidence.observation: Strong a-gildan/-geldan/-gieldan/-gyldan has geald/guldon/golden and includes reward, repay, requite. Separate weak a-giltan has gilte/gilt and means sin, fail, do wrong.
a-gyldan expressly gives thu gyltst/he gylt and geald/guldon/golden. Dative recipients occur in repayment examples. Separate a-gyltan/-giltan has gylte/gilte and gylt/gilt, fail in duty or sin.
Reward is the noun med; requite is forgieldan(III.104). The vocabulary supplies no independent support for agyltan as the verb reward.
Strong gieldan/geald/guldon/golden is explicitly tabulated under104. Prefixing does not turn this into weak class113.
Section113 describes weak de/te preterits retaining the stem vowel, with hieran, fyllan, cyssan, settan and sendan among its examples. It cannot describe strong gyldan/geald/guldon/golden.

additional_primary_corroboration.original_identifier: Matthew16.27, left/first column and its A apparatus
additional_primary_corroboration.observation: Leftcolumn prints mannes Sunu ys to cumenne and then agylt æghwylcum be hys agenum worce. Apparatus at bottom explicitly gives Ch.xvi.v.27,6.A.cumanne and21.A.B.weorce. This corroborates the bounded impending-coming phrase, selected cumanne variant, contracted reward verb and dative recipient. The new model is not presented as an exact quotation of this differently spelled parallel.
